title: When the Will Turns Anew
premise: Estate lawyer Gideon Okafor is hired by a dying heiress, Marguerite Hale, who pays a fortune in advance for one task: prove, before it happens, that her family will murder her for her inheritance. When she is found dead within a week, ruled a natural death, Gideon realizes the will he notarized is the murder weapon — a document designed to make her death inevitable and profitable. As he investigates outside the law, he discovers Marguerite staged her own poisoning as a test, leaving clues only a lawyer would read, and the real killer is the family's trusted attorney who has forged wills for decades. In the climax, Gideon traps him by filing a deliberately flawed codicil, forcing the killer to alter the estate record and expose himself; justice arrives not through the police, but through the law Gideon wields like a blade.
about_author: Odile Voss is the pen name of a former probate clerk who spent eleven years in the back rooms of estate law before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about paperwork, power, and the quiet violence of inheritance from a coastal town whose name she declines to share.

chapters.title: The Client Who Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Gideon Okafor's POV. A frail, sharp-eyed Marguerite Hale arrives at his office with a cashier's check covering fees for a case she describes in strange terms: prove a murder that hasn't happened yet. She refuses to name the killer. The beat is uneasy fascination — Gideon takes the retainer against his better judgment.

chapters.title: Terms of the Dead
chapters.summary: Marguerite dictates a new will, cutting out her three adult children and leaving everything to a trust Gideon must administer. She insists on a clause that triggers full disclosure 'upon my unnatural death.' Gideon's POV; the emotional beat is dread disguised as professional routine.

chapters.title: Seven Days
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, her final days. She moves through Hale House cataloguing small betrayals — her son's debts, her daughter's surveillance, the family attorney Aldous Wren's too-frequent visits. She leaves a sealed envelope in the library wall. The beat is calm resolve, a woman arranging her own chessboard.

chapters.title: Natural Causes
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Six days after signing, Marguerite is dead; the physician certifies heart failure. At the funeral, the children are composed, Wren flawless. But Gideon finds the will's trigger clause means he now holds a document worth millions — and someone at the reception watches him with open calculation.

chapters.title: The File That Reads Back
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Reviewing Marguerite's papers, he notices her medication was switched weeks before her death — and that whoever did it knew exactly which records the coroner would and wouldn't request. Someone understands investigative procedure intimately. The beat shifts from grief to cold alarm.

chapters.title: Three Heirs, One Motive
chapters.summary: Gideon interviews the children under pretext of estate administration. Son Theodore is drowning in debt, daughter Camille hired a private nurse she then dismissed, youngest Elias hasn't spoken to his mother in a decade. Each has motive; each has an alibi that is slightly too neat. Gideon's POV; the beat is mounting suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Wall Kept
chapters.summary: Gideon breaks into Hale House's library and retrieves Marguerite's sealed envelope: her own handwritten investigation into her children, plus a single line — 'If I am wrong, it will be the one who taught you the forms.' Gideon's POV. The beat is vertigo: the killer may be a fellow lawyer.

chapters.title: Aldous Wren, Esquire
chapters.summary: Gideon probes Wren's history and finds a pattern: three past estates where heirs died within months of signing, each ruled natural. Wren is charming, unhurried, and clearly enjoys the conversation. Gideon's POV; the beat is a duel conducted entirely in courtesies.

chapters.title: The Coroner's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Detective Ines Marchetti's POV. She notices an anonymous inquiry into Hale toxicology records and pulls the file — traces of a cardiac-suppressant, dismissed as contamination. She begins her own quiet inquiry, suspicious of the estate lawyer who keeps appearing at the edges. The beat is professional instinct sharpening.

chapters.title: Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He realizes anything he finds is tainted — he's a beneficiary's trustee investigating his own case. He decides to work off the books: breaking into Wren's office after hours, he photographs decades of client ledgers and finds altered codicils. The beat is the point of no return.

chapters.title: Theodore's Confession
chapters.summary: Theodore Hale, drunk and terrified, tells Gideon he was approached weeks ago with an offer: contest the will, and someone would make his debts vanish. He never learned who. Gideon's POV; the beat is pity curdling — the killer recruited the heirs as cover.

chapters.title: Marchetti's Warning
chapters.summary: Detective Marchetti confronts Gideon, laying out how suspicious he looks: retained by the victim, present at every anomaly, now caught in Wren's office by an alarm report. She gives him forty-eight hours before she arrests him. Gideon's POV; the beat is the walls closing in.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Gideon rereads the trigger clause and realizes Marguerite embedded a legal riddle — a misdated exhibit that only makes sense if read against Wren's own drafting style. She anticipated her killer and left the proof where only a lawyer would look. Gideon's POV; the beat is awe and grief entwined.

chapters.title: The Forger's Hand
chapters.summary: Gideon compares Wren's drafting habits across forty years — a distinctive double-space, a favored Latin phrase — and matches them to the 'old' codicil that disinherited Marguerite's first husband before his convenient death. The pattern spans generations. Gideon's POV; the beat is horror at the scale.

chapters.title: Camille's Bargain
chapters.summary: Camille Hale's POV. She reveals she hired the private nurse to protect her mother, then dismissed her under pressure from Wren, who threatened to expose her forged signature on an earlier document. She agrees to testify — if Gideon can guarantee the trust protects her. The beat is fear traded for courage.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, racing the clock. Marchetti prepares his warrant while he drafts the trap: a codicil containing a deliberately flawed residuary clause, filed with the probate court, that Wren cannot resist 'correcting.' The beat is feverish, meticulous tension — the murder weapon is now paperwork.

chapters.title: The Correction
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, briefly. He finds the flawed filing and, unable to leave an imperfect instrument on record, alters it — using the same forged-attestation technique from decades of prior crimes, captured by a process server Gideon hired to witness the filing. The beat is arrogance meeting the snare.

chapters.title: Probate at Midnight
chapters.summary: Climax. Gideon presents the evidence to Marchetti: the forged codicils, the witnessed alteration, Marguerite's riddle, and the exhumation order for the first husband. Wren, cornered at a probate hearing he assumed he controlled, unravels with terrifying eloquence. The beat is the trap springing shut.

chapters.title: What the Dead Are Owed
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Wren is charged across four decades of cases; families Gideon never met receive letters reopening their estates. Marguerite's children, cleared of murder but not of smallness, must live with the will she wrote. The beat is justice that feels earned but not sweet.

chapters.title: The Trust
chapters.summary: Gideon executes Marguerite's trust: the bulk goes to a legal fund for victims of estate fraud, with modest provision for each child. Camille thanks him; Theodore does not. Marchetti closes the file, acknowledging he broke a dozen laws to make one law mean something. The beat is quiet reckoning.

chapters.title: A Will Turns Anew
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, weeks later. He reopens his office, changes his intake forms, and takes on a pro bono case for an elderly man whose caregiver keeps asking about his accounts. The final beat: vigilance as inheritance — Marguerite's lesson carried forward.

chapters.title: Epilogue: The Envelope in the Wall
chapters.summary: Final image from Marguerite's posthumous letter, read aloud by Gideon to an empty office: she never expected to survive, only to be proven right. She asks that the last line of her file read not 'deceased' but 'correct.' The beat is elegy — a life that ended as an argument, and won.
